chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Muhammad ibn Mas'ud al-Ta'i, who said:

I said to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him): 'My mother gave charity to me with a house of hers,' or he said, 'with her share in a house.' So she said to me, 'Secure it for yourself.' So I wrote to her that I had bought it, and that she had sold it to me and taken possession of the price. So when she died, the inheritors said, 'Swear an oath that you bought it and paid the price.' So if I were to swear to them, I would take it, and if I did not swear to them, they would not give me anything.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'So swear to them and take what she made for you.'
ai.seo_question: How does one secure a gift from a parent against other heirs' claims according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith illustrates the Shia juristic principle of 'takhrij al-mal' (extracting wealth) through a legal fiction, where a gift is disguised as a sale to protect it from other heirs' claims. The Imam’s directive to swear the oath validates the son's possession, highlighting the practical flexibility in Shia inheritance law to preserve parental intent while navigating the rigid rules of statutory shares (fara'id).
